## Introduction

Parallel Coordinate Plots (PCP) are a powerful visualization technique for exploring multivariate data.

- Each variable is a vertical axis
- Each observation is a connected line across the axes
- Useful for spotting patterns across **many dimensions at once**

<!-- ## Load Libraries -->

<!-- Before running this code, install 3 packages: -->

<!-- - `tidyverse` – main package for data science -->
<!-- - `GGally` – provides `ggparcoord()` for PCPs -->
<!-- - `plotly` – for interactive graphics -->

```{r load-libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(GGally)      # For ggparcoord
library(plotly)      # For interactive plots
library(kableExtra)  # for tables
```

## Data

Data set used for the sake of the exercise (generated).

```{r generate-data}
set.seed(123)

# data <- tibble(
#   id = 1:10,
#   sex = c(rep("Men", 6), rep("Women", 4)),
# 
#   # Age: Men older (45-55), Women younger (25-35)
#   age = c(48, 52, 45, 50, 47, 54,
#           28, 32, 26, 30),
# 
#   # Education: Men lower (12-14 yrs), Women higher (16-18 yrs)
#   education = c(12, 14, 13, 12, 14, 13,
#                 18, 17, 18, 16),
# 
#   # Income: Men high (70k-90k), Women moderate (40k-55k)
#   income = c(85000, 78000, 82000, 90000, 75000, 88000,
#              48000, 52000, 45000, 50000)
# )
```


```{r}
N = 1000


generate_pcp_data <- function(Nobs) {
 set.seed(123)
 n_men   <- round(Nobs * 0.6)
 n_women <- Nobs - n_men

  tibble(
    id  = 1:Nobs,
    sex = c(rep("Men", n_men), rep("Women", n_women)),
    age = round(c(rnorm(n_men,   mean = 49.3,  sd = 5),
                  rnorm(n_women, mean = 49.3,    sd = 6))),
    education = round(c(rnorm(n_men,   mean = 13,    sd = 0.9),
                        rnorm(n_women, mean = 17.25, sd = 0.96))),
    income = round(c(rnorm(n_men,   mean = 83000, sd = 4700),
                     rnorm(n_women, mean = 65750, sd = 5100)))
  )
}

data <- generate_pcp_data(N)
```




```{r write-data}
#| eval: false
#| include: false
write.csv(select(data, age, education, income),
          paste0("Data/PCPData-",Nobs,".csv"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
data %>% 
  select(-sex) %>%
  select(-1) %>%   # Remove id
  kable(caption = paste0("Data Set, N=",N),
    align = "c",
    digits = 2
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),
    full_width = FALSE
  )
```


## Basic Parallel Coordinate Plot

```{r basic-pcp}
#| fig-align: center
data_pcp <- data %>%
  select(id, age, education, income)


# Computing values for axes as workaround for scaling
vars <- names(data_pcp)[2:4]

range_labels <- data.frame(
  x = seq_along(vars),
  min_val = sapply(vars, function(v) min(data_pcp[[v]], na.rm = TRUE)),
  max_val = sapply(vars, function(v) max(data_pcp[[v]], na.rm = TRUE))
)

ggparcoord(
  data_pcp,
  columns = c(2,3,4),
  #groupColumn = "id",
  showPoints = TRUE,
  scale = "uniminmax"
) +
  labs(
    title = "Income, Age and Education",
    x = NULL, y = "Scaled Values (0-1)"
  ) +
  geom_line(color = "orange")+
  labs(title = "PCP with points", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
 theme_minimal() +
 theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.y = element_blank()) +
  geom_text(data = range_labels, aes(x = x, y = -0.06, label = round(min_val, 1)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3, color = "grey30") +
  geom_text(data = range_labels, aes(x = x, y = 1.06, label = round(max_val, 1)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3, color = "grey30") +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off", ylim = c(-0.1, 1.1))

```

::: {.notes}
Notice how the lines form two distinct groups, even though we haven't colored them.
:::

## Enhanced PCP with Transparency

Adding transparency (`alpha`) helps reveal overlapping patterns.

```{r enhanced-pcp}
#| fig-align: center
ggparcoord(
  data_pcp,
  columns = c(2,3,4),
  #groupColumn = "id",
  scale = "uniminmax",
  alphaLines = 1/N  # This parameter is overpassed by next one (alpha)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth =  ifelse(N >10,  1.5, 1.2),
            color = "orange",
            alpha =  ifelse(N >10,  20/N, 0.5) ) +
  labs(title = "With transparency", x = NULL, y = "Scaled Values") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Interactive Version {.smaller}

Using interactivity and applying a color to the two groups

```{r interactive-pcp}

plot_data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    color_code = ifelse(sex == "Men", 0, 1),
    label = paste0(
      "ID: ", id, "<br>",
      "Sex: ", sex, "<br>",
      "Age: ", age, "<br>",
      "Education: ", education, " years<br>",
      "Income: $", format(income, big.mark = ",")
    )
  )

n <- nrow(plot_data)

fig <- plot_ly(
  data = plot_data,
  type = 'parcoords',
  line = list(
    color = rep(0, n),
    colorscale = list(c(0, '#999999'), c(1, '#999999')),
    showscale = FALSE,
    width = 4
  ),
  dimensions = list(
    list(label = 'Income ($)', values = ~income, range = c(50000, 95000)),
    list(label = 'Age', values = ~age, range = c(35, 65)),
    list(label = 'Education (years)', values = ~education, range = c(10, 20))
  )
)

fig <- fig %>%
  layout(
    title = list(text = "Parallel Coordinate Plot", font = list(size = 16), y = 0.98),
    annotations = list(list(
      text = "Drag axes to filter",
      showarrow = FALSE, xref = "paper", yref = "paper",
      x = 0.8, y = 1.15, font = list(size = 9, color = "grey40")
    )),
    updatemenus = list(list(
      type = "buttons", direction = "right",
      x = 0.5, xanchor = "center", y = 1.3, yanchor = "top",
      buttons = list(
        list(method = "restyle",
             args = list(list("line.color" = list(rep(0, n)),
                               "line.colorscale" = list(list(c(0, '#999999'), c(1, '#999999'))))),
             label = "No Color"),
        list(method = "restyle",
             args = list(list("line.color" = list(plot_data$color_code),
                               "line.colorscale" = list(list(c(0, '#3498DB'), c(1, '#E74C3C'))))),
             label = "Color")
      )
    )),
    margin = list(l = 100, r = 100, t = 110, b = 30),
    height = 400,
    autosize = TRUE,
    plot_bgcolor = '#f8f9fa',
    paper_bgcolor = 'white'
  )

fig
```

## PCP with revealed group (hidden)

Coloring the lines by sex makes the two groups visually distinct.

```{r pcp-colored}
#| fig-align: center
data_with_sex <- data %>%
  select(id, sex,  education,income,  age)

# Computing values for axes
vars <- names(data_with_sex)[3:5]

range_labels <- data.frame(
  x = seq_along(vars),
  min_val = sapply(vars, function(v) min(data_with_sex[[v]], na.rm = TRUE)),
  max_val = sapply(vars, function(v) max(data_with_sex[[v]], na.rm = TRUE))
)

# PCP
fig.sex <- ggparcoord(
  data_with_sex,
  columns = 3:5,
  groupColumn = "sex",  # for color"
  splineFactor = 1,  # Straight line
  scale = "uniminmax",
  alphaLines = ifelse(N >10,  20/N, 0.5)
) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Men" = "#3498DB", "Women" = "#E74C3C")) +
  labs(title = "Two Distinct Groups", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
 theme(legend.position = "top",
        axis.text.y = element_blank()) +
  geom_text(data = range_labels, aes(x = x, y = -0.06, label = round(min_val, 1)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3, color = "grey30") +
  geom_text(data = range_labels, aes(x = x, y = 1.06, label = round(max_val, 1)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 3, color = "grey30") +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off", ylim = c(-0.1, 1.1))


fig.sex
```

## Analysis by sex

```{r summary-stats}
data %>%
  group_by(sex) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_education = mean(education),
    avg_income = mean(income),
    avg_age = mean(age),
     n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 1,
    col.names = c("Sex", "Avg Education", "Avg Income","Avg Age",  "N")
  )
```


```{r}
fig.sex
```

## Key Insights

1. **Two Distinct Patterns**: Even without labeling sex, two clear groups emerge
2. **Education–Income paradox**: Higher education correlates with lower income (women)
3. **Group Characteristics**
   - Men:  moderate education, higher income
   - Women: higher education, lower income, a bit younger. 

## Conclusion

Parallel Coordinate Plots are excellent for:

- Visualizing multivariate relationships
- Identifying patterns and clusters
- Exploring high-dimensional data
- Interactive data exploration

The key advantage: seeing **multiple dimensions** simultaneously, making hidden patterns visible.
